top_choice_rationale: P002 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is my first choice, but narrowly over P001. It rests on a transparent, credibly identified design that has been replicated across countries. The qualitative finding of concentrated, persistent local labour-market losses from import competition has survived about a decade of scrutiny, even as magnitudes and shift-share inference remain debated. The three names are the joint authors of the central papers, so attribution is clean under the three-name cap. I would anchor the citation on the trade-shock and local-labour-market evidence and treat technological change only as context, because the task-based lineage (Levy, Murnane, Katz, Acemoglu) is not owned by these three. P001 (Kiyotaki, Moore) is a very close second: its attribution is cleaner and its record longer, but direct empirical validation of the collateral-amplification mechanism is more indirect and its marginal case after the 2022 prize is not verified here. I weigh direct identification of a first-order question slightly above conceptual generality and age. I would accept P001 without objection. P003 is a substantive and mature methods advance, but it depends on functional-form and instrument assumptions and rests on a narrower base of support. A prize in 2026 is preferable to no award.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile for any candidate on the slate (Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Kiyotaki, Moore, Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn). My collaborators (V-Dem core team, Rothstein, Holmberg, Hadenius, Dahlström, Lapuente, Bäck, Lindvall) are not credited. I disclose that I am a political scientist, so research on the political consequences of trade exposure is adjacent to P002. My causal-inference orientation may lead me to weight direct identification above conceptual generality. I am a Stockholm University colleague, in a different department, of committee members Hassler, Krusell and Boppart. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
